output:
**Dear Kelechi,**

You said if I was serious about you becoming a maths teacher, I had to put it in writing. Not a voice note. A proper letter you could read on the train. So here you go. I’ve even posted it to Croydon, because apparently after nine years of spreadsheets you need your career advice delivered by Royal Mail.

I’m not asking you to resign, sign anything, or turn up at school on Monday with a box of exercise books. I’m asking you to come with me to the open evening on **Thursday 19 November at 6pm**, at the training partnership in Lewisham. That’s all. We can listen, ask questions, find out what the salaried route actually involves, and then go home. You can decide it’s not for you. But at least you’ll be deciding based on more than my big mouth at your birthday.

You’ve been a quantity surveyor for nine years. You’re good at it, I know. But every time we talk about work, it sounds like the same spreadsheet has been following you around for the better part of a decade. And on your last birthday, you said you wanted to do something that mattered before you turn 40. I remembered. Annoying of me, I know.

I also remember what you were like at Moremi before exams. You got an A in further maths, yes, but that’s not the point. You were tutoring half the hostel, and somehow people came away understanding the thing instead of feeling stupid for not getting it already. You’ve always been patient when you explain something. You make people laugh without making them the joke. That combination is rarer than you think, and it’s exactly the sort of thing that makes a difference in a classroom.

Exhibit A: my nephew and the fractions at Christmas. You explained them using portions of jollof rice on plates, and he still talks about it. I’m not saying you must teach every lesson with a tray of rice—though I’d support the innovation—but you found a way to make fractions feel real to him. That’s teaching, Kelechi. Not just knowing the answer, but finding a way for someone else to see it too.

And yes, I know a classroom is not a hostel room full of your friends. The school where I teach in Peckham has about 1,100 kids, and we’ve had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups since September. They need stability, and they need adults who can explain things calmly and make them feel capable. I’m not pretending that one brilliant teacher fixes everything. But you could be the person who helps a kid go from “I can’t do maths” to “wait, I can.”

Last month, a Year 11 boy called Damola finally got simultaneous equations after three weeks of wrestling with them. He looked at the page and shouted, “Is that all??” The whole class clapped. It was a small moment, probably forgotten by everyone else by the next lesson. But he’ll remember that feeling: the thing he thought was impossible suddenly making sense. That’s the bit of this job that keeps me here.

Now for the part where I don’t try to sell you a classroom as a magical land of grateful children and endless inspirational breakthroughs. Teaching is hard. Marking can feel endless. Some days behaviour is pure wahala, and you’ll go home tired in a way a spreadsheet has never managed. There’s paperwork, there are difficult conversations, and there will be lessons where you give your best explanation and get blank faces in return. I won’t lie to you about any of that. You’d hate me if I did.

I cried in the car park twice in my first term when I started in 2019. Twice. I’m not polishing the story for recruitment purposes. I was overwhelmed and wondered whether I’d made a terrible mistake. It gets better—not because the hard parts disappear, but because you learn the job, find your feet, and start to see the good moments build up. You get better at handling the rough days. And then, every so often, a kid like Damola makes the whole room clap over simultaneous equations, and you remember why you chose this.

The route I’m talking about is salaried: you get paid while you train. It’s one year, with the training starting in September 2027. There would be a pay drop in the first year, and I’m not going to pretend that doesn’t matter. You’d want to look properly at the numbers and ask what the salary, holidays and pension would mean for you. Pay goes up, and there are the school holidays too—but don’t choose this because I’ve made it sound like a financial hack. Come and hear the details, then work out whether it makes sense for your life.

And before you say you’re too old to switch: you’re 34, not 84. There’s a woman in my department who started at 41. Nobody took her aside to tell her she’d missed the teacher deadline. You have years of work ahead of you, and you’ve already said you want those years to add up to something. Teaching isn’t the only way to do that, obviously. But it could be one way that suits the person you already are.

I’m teasing you because I know you: you’ll probably say you’re “just looking” and then interrogate them about the training structure like you’re pricing a new development. Fine. Ask all the questions. Ask about the workload, the money, the course, the school placements, the hard bits. Be as suspicious as you like. That is what the open evening is for.

So, my actual proposal is small: come to Lewisham with me on **19 November at 6pm**. We’ll listen, ask questions, and leave without committing to a thing. Applications for next September are opening soon, so it seems sensible to find out what the option is before it’s in front of you. You don’t have to become a teacher. You don’t have to decide that night. Just come and see.

You’ve spent nine years checking other people’s costings. Maybe it’s time to find out whether you’d rather help someone work out what they’re capable of.

I’ll go with you. I’ll even buy you a drink afterwards, though if you ask me to explain the pension projections over it, I’m charging a consultancy fee.

Your friend,  
**[Your name]**
